title: Very large cities, city size and the urban hierarchy

stimuli.title: Population of selected very large cities, 2025

map.label: Graduated symbol map of seven very large cities in 2025, five of them in Asia (Jakarta, Tokyo, New Delhi, Shanghai, Manila), one in Africa (Cairo) and one in South America (Sao Paulo)
map.source: UN DESA, World Urbanization Prospects 2025 (2025 estimates, Degree of Urbanisation method)

stimuli.title: The five largest cities of Country Z

table.caption: Country Z, an invented country (invented data for practice). Offices of global firms: offices of the world's 100 largest finance, law and advertising firms.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Using Source 1, identify the world region where most of the very large cities shown are located.

rubric.point: Identifies Asia (or South, Southeast and East Asia).

parts.sample: Asia: five of the seven very large cities shown are in South, Southeast or East Asia.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Using Source 1, describe the difference between a megacity and a metacity, using one city shown as an example.

rubric.point: Describes a megacity as 10 million or more and a metacity as 20 million or more, with a correct example from the map.
accept: Sao Paulo, about 18.9 million, is a megacity but not a metacity
Jakarta, about 41.9 million, is a metacity because it has more than 20 million

parts.sample: A megacity has 10 million people or more, while a metacity has 20 million or more; Sao Paulo, with about 18.9 million in 2025, is a megacity but not a metacity, whereas Jakarta, with about 41.9 million, is a metacity.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain why most of the very large cities shown in Source 1 are in lower- and middle-income countries.

rubric.point: Explains rapid growth from rural-to-urban migration and/or natural increase, with the link to city size.
accept: young people move from villages to cities for jobs, and births exceed deaths, so these cities grow very large
high rural-to-urban migration adds millions of residents each decade, so the cities pass 10 or 20 million

parts.sample: In these countries many young people move from villages to cities in search of work, and births in the cities still far outnumber deaths, so their largest cities add millions of people each decade and grow into megacities and metacities.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain one limitation of Source 1 for comparing the populations of the world's very large cities.

rubric.point: Explains a limitation with its consequence, such as: a city's count depends on where its edge is drawn, so sources using other definitions rank cities differently; or the map shows only selected cities, so it cannot show every very large city; or it shows one year, so it cannot show which cities are growing fastest.
accept: city populations depend on how the edge of the urban area is drawn, so another source (such as older UN tables using each country's own definitions) can give different numbers and rankings
the map shows only seven selected cities, so very large cities that are left out cannot be compared
the map shows only 2025, so it cannot show how fast each city is growing

parts.sample: The populations depend on where each city's edge is drawn. This map uses one satellite-based method, while older UN tables used each country's own city boundaries and ranked Tokyo first, so the same cities can have different sizes and ranks in another source.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Using Source 2, explain whether Country Z's cities fit the rank-size rule or show a primate city.

rubric.point: Explains with values that Z1 is far larger than the rule predicts relative to Z2 (or Z2 far smaller), so Country Z has a primate city.
accept: the rule expects Z2 to have 5 million, but it has 2, so Z1 is a primate city
Z1 has 10 million, five times Z2, so it is a primate city rather than a rank-size pattern

parts.sample: Country Z shows a primate city, because the rank-size rule would expect Z2 to have about 5 million people (10 / 2), but it has only 2 million, so Z1 is five times larger than the next city and dominates the country.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Using Source 2, explain how Z1's position in the urban hierarchy can affect smaller cities in Country Z, linking the global and national scales.

rubric.point: Explains that Z1, with most global firm offices, links Country Z to the world economy, so decisions, investment or new ideas reach the smaller cities through it (for example by hierarchical diffusion).
accept: global firms make decisions in Z1, so investment and jobs in Z2 to Z5 depend on choices made there
new products and ideas arrive from world cities in Z1 first and then spread down to Z2 to Z5, so the smaller cities adopt them later

parts.sample: Z1 holds 85 of the global firm offices, so it links Country Z to world cities at the global scale; new products, investment and decisions arrive in Z1 first and then spread down the hierarchy to Z2 through Z5 at the national scale, which leaves the smaller cities dependent on choices made in Z1.

parts.label: G
parts.prompt: Using Source 2, explain the degree to which a primate city such as Z1 benefits the economic development of the whole country.

rubric.point: States a degree first (high, moderate or low), then explains with evidence from Source 2 both how Z1 helps (its global firm offices draw investment and link the country to the world economy) and how a primate city can hold back other regions (investment and migrants gather in Z1 while Z2 to Z5 lag), or justifies a one-sided degree.
accept: to a moderate degree: Z1's 85 global firm offices bring investment and links to the world, but money, jobs and migrants gather there, so Z2 to Z5 (only 1 to 9 offices) are left behind
to a low degree: most global investment stays in Z1, so the gap between Z1 and the smaller cities grows and other regions develop slowly

parts.sample: To a moderate degree. Z1 holds 85 of the offices of global firms, so it brings foreign investment, jobs and links to the world economy into Country Z. But the smaller cities have only 1 to 9 such offices, so investment, jobs and migrants keep gathering in Z1, which crowds the capital and leaves the other regions behind.
